content: Estrogen injections carry a significant risk of increasing the likelihood of developing endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining. The longer you use estrogen, the higher this risk becomes. If you have not undergone a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus), your doctor will likely prescribe a progestin to be taken alongside the estrogen injection. This combination may reduce the risk of endometrial cancer but could increase the risk of other health issues, such as breast cancer. Before starting estrogen injections, inform your doctor if you have a history of cancer or if you experience unusual vaginal bleeding. Your doctor will monitor you closely during and after treatment to ensure you do not develop endometrial cancer. Studies have shown that women who take estrogen combined with progestins orally have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the lungs or legs, breast cancer, and dementia (a decline in cognitive abilities). Women using estrogen injections, either alone or with progestins, may also face an increased risk of these conditions. Inform your doctor if you smoke, have had a heart attack or stroke within the past year, or if you or a family member has a history of blood clots or breast cancer. Additionally, let your doctor know if you have or have had high blood pressure, high cholesterol or fat levels, diabetes, heart disease, lupus, breast lumps, or an abnormal mammogram. Be vigilant for symptoms that may indicate serious health conditions. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience sudden, severe headaches; severe vomiting; speech difficulties; dizziness or fainting; sudden vision loss or double vision; weakness or numbness in an arm or leg; crushing chest pain or heaviness; coughing up blood; sudden shortness of breath; difficulty thinking clearly, remembering, or learning new things; breast lumps or changes; nipple discharge; or pain, tenderness, or redness in one leg. To minimize the risk of serious health problems while using estrogen injections, do not use them alone or with progestins to prevent heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, or dementia. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to control your symptoms. Discuss with your doctor every 3–6 months whether you should lower your dose or discontinue the medication. Perform monthly breast self-exams and have an annual mammogram and breast exam by a doctor to detect breast cancer early. Your doctor may recommend more frequent exams based on your personal or family medical history. Inform your doctor if you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, as they may advise stopping estrogen injections 4–6 weeks beforehand to reduce the risk of blood clots. Regularly discuss the risks and benefits of estrogen injections with your doctor. Estrogen injections, such as estradiol cypionate and estradiol valerate, are used to treat hot flashes and vaginal symptoms (dryness, itching, burning) associated with menopause. However, women needing treatment solely for vaginal symptoms should consider alternative therapies. These injections may also be used to treat low estrogen levels in younger women who do not produce enough estrogen naturally. Estradiol valerate may be used to alleviate symptoms of certain types of prostate cancer, while conjugated estrogens are used to treat abnormal vaginal bleeding caused by hormonal imbalances. Estrogen injections work by replacing the estrogen normally produced by the body. Estradiol cypionate and estradiol valerate are long-acting forms of estrogen injections administered into a muscle, typically every 3–4 weeks by a healthcare professional. When used for prostate cancer symptoms, estradiol valerate is usually injected every 1–2 weeks. Conjugated estrogens come as a powder to be mixed with sterile water and injected into a muscle or vein, often as a single dose. A second dose may be given 6–12 hours later if needed to control vaginal bleeding. If you are using estrogen injections for hot flashes, your symptoms should improve within 1–5 days after the injection. Notify your doctor if your symptoms do not improve during this time. Before using estrogen injections, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to estrogen products or any of the ingredients in the injection. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some may interact with estrogen. Mention any herbal products, especially St. John’s wort. Inform your doctor if you have or have had yellowing of the skin or eyes during pregnancy or estrogen treatment, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, asthma, migraines, seizures, porphyria, abnormal calcium levels, or thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, or pancreatic disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor immediately. Discuss with your doctor whether you should consume grapefruit or grapefruit juice while using this medication, as it may interact with estrogen. If you miss a scheduled dose of estrogen injection, contact your doctor as soon as possible. Estrogen injections may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include breast pain or tenderness, upset stomach, vomiting, weight changes, dizziness, nervousness, depression, irritability, changes in sexual desire, hair loss, unwanted hair growth, dark spots on the face, difficulty wearing contact lenses, leg cramps, vaginal irritation, or discharge. Notify your doctor if these symptoms are severe or persistent. Serious side effects include bulging eyes, stomach pain or swelling, loss of appetite, weakness, yellowing of the skin or eyes, joint pain, uncontrollable movements, rash or blisters, hives, itching, swelling of the face or extremities, hoarseness, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. Estrogen may increase the risk of ovarian cancer or gallbladder disease requiring surgery. Children receiving high doses of estrogen for extended periods may experience slowed or halted growth. Discuss these risks with your doctor. In case of an overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual collapses or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding. Keep all appointments with your doctor and inform laboratory personnel that you are using estrogen injections before undergoing any tests.
